claim: The safety gear stops a falling car by gripping the guide rails, and is tripped by the overspeed governor or by breakage of the suspension
source_quote: capable of stopping a car carrying the rated load … at the tripping speed of the overspeed governor, or if the suspension devices break, by gripping the guide rails
note: EN 81-20:2020 5.6.2.1.1.1 (via AS 1735.1.2:2021). The wrong model ('slams on as hard as it can') is the viewer's, not a claim. VO v5: 'It does not care why you are too fast. A snapped rope, or anything else.' (tripped at governor speed, or by breakage of the suspension).

claim: The safety gear is not set off electrically: Europe's code forbids tripping it by electric, hydraulic or pneumatic devices (VO: 'nothing electric, and no fluid or air pressure')
source_quote: Safety gears shall not be tripped by devices, which operate electrically, hydraulically or pneumatically.
note: EN 81-20:2020 5.6.2.1.6.4. VO v5 says 'The European standard for elevators'.

claim: In the example elevator the car falls for a fraction of a second (about 0.2 s from rest to a 2.0 m/s trip) and stops within about a meter (0.5 m typical, 1.2 m late-trip worst case)
source_quote: tripping … at a speed at least equal to 115 % of the rated speed and less than … 1,25 · v + 0,25/v; the maximum distance between tripping points … shall not exceed 250 mm
note: DERIVED in research/model.py from EN 81-20 5.6.2.2.1.1/.2 and 5.6.2.1.3 for an example 1.6 m/s lift; HUD label MODEL. VO says 'in a typical elevator'.

claim: An elevator car hangs on several ropes (US codes: at least three for traction elevators)
source_quote: The minimum number of hoisting ropes used is three for traction elevators and two for drum-type elevators.
note: Seattle Building Code 2018, 3011.6.12.4 (ASME A17.1-derived); second: calcimator elevator rope calculator cites the same ASME minimum. VO hedges 'often'. VO v4: 'usually has several'.

claim: Each suspension rope must be many times stronger than its share of the load (factor of safety about 7.6 to 12)
source_quote: The factor of safety of the suspension wire ropes shall not be less than shown on the following table.
note: Table values 7.60 (50 fpm) to 11.90 (1400–2000 fpm), passenger. EN 81-20 uses 12 (3+ ropes) / 16 (2 ropes) per Elevator World. 'many times' covers both. Not said in VO v6 (kept for the picture: a factor-of-safety bar may appear).

claim: The overspeed governor is a rope-driven wheel: a rope loop tied to the car drives it, so it turns with the car's speed
source_quote: is also connected to the elevator car 12, ensuring that the angular velocity of the tripping sheave 18 is related to the speed of the elevator car 12
note: Otis US 8,931,598 B2 background. Second: Bode manual (rope attached to the car's safety frame).

claim: The governor rope runs down to a weighted (tensioning) pulley in the pit
source_quote: the overspeed governor rope shall be tensioned by a pulley with a tensioning weight
note: EN 81-20 5.6.2.2.1.3 d). 'In the pit' is the usual layout (Bode manual: governor rope pulley in the shaft pit). VO v6 says 'down to the bottom of the shaft and back up'; the weighted pulley is drawn, not said.

claim: In a classic governor, flyweights held in by springs swing outward with speed (centrifugal force)
source_quote: a centrifugal force acting to propel the masses away from the sheave axis of rotation … The coupler commonly includes a spring connected between the sheave and one of the masses
note: VO: 'In a classic governor' (Bode uses a pendulum on a square cam: same principle, different hardware).

claim: The governor trips at a set speed at least 15 % above rated speed
source_quote: tripping of the overspeed governor for the safety gear shall occur at a speed at least equal to 115 % of the rated speed

claim: When it trips, the governor wheel locks and its rope stops while the car keeps moving; the rope is hooked to the safety-gear lever on the car, so the car's motion past the stopped rope pulls the lever
source_quote: the pendulum blocks the overspeed governor wheel. It is mechanically blocked and cannot rotate anymore. The lift car continues moving in the shaft, the overspeed governor rope, guided in the wedge groove, blocks and engages the safety gear of the lift.
note: Bode manual 2024. 'Lever on the car': BF manual describes governor-rope tripping devices with lever arms at the gear.

claim: Many governors also operate a switch first to cut the motor
source_quote: Pre-cut-off switch
note: Bode manual (pre-cut-off switch; electrical tripping set below the mechanical trip). Also EN 81-20 5.6.2.1.5: an electric safety device stops the machine at gear operation.

claim: Progressive safety gear closes braking elements on the rail from both sides (in pairs), activated by a movable wedge, with disc springs setting the braking force
source_quote: a combination of disc springs and braking elements always in pairs … activated by a movable tripping wedge … The braking force is adjustable by the disc spring assembly.
note: Wittur CSGB. The drawing is a SIMPLIFIED generic wedge gear; labelled as a model.

claim: The rail stands still while the car falls; once a wedge touches it, friction holds the wedge back so it slides higher into the narrowing slot
source_quote: the frictional force further pulls the wedge to move upward
note: Otis US 10,407,278 B2 (self-locking angle 5–11°: the slot narrows). 'Rail rushes upward' is relative motion seen from the car.

claim: Example trip speed about 2 m/s; stopping that in 2 cm would mean about 10 g
source_quote: less than … 1,25 · v + 0,25/v … for progressive safety gear for rated speeds exceeding 1,0 m/s
note: DERIVED: 2.0 m/s inside the 1.84–2.16 m/s window of a 1.6 m/s lift; a = v²/2d = 100 m/s² = 10.2 g (research/model.py). HUD: MODEL.

claim: In 1854 in New York (Crystal Palace), Elisha Otis stood on a platform high in the air and had its rope cut
source_quote: Orders were few until May 1854 when, at the Crystal Palace in New York City, he demonstrated his elevator by riding the platform high in the air and ordering the rope cut.
note: Second: Elevator World, 'Elisha Otis' Improved Elevator': exhibited at the New York Crystal Palace in 1854. 'All safe, gentlemen' is unverified (Elevator World): not used. VO v6: 'stood on' (Britannica: 'riding the platform high in the air'); 'rode' was misheard as 'wrote' by speech-to-text and was dropped for clarity.

claim: Otis's safety: when the rope was cut, springs threw pawls (hooks) into racks (teeth) along the guides, holding the platform
source_quote: In case the rope G should break in hoisting the loaded platform D, the pawls f f, in consequence of being released from the pull of said rope, will immediately be thrown in connection with the racks C C by the springs
note: US 31,128 (1861; the 1854 device per Elevator World: 'ratchet-and-pawl safety engaged when the hoisting rope was cut'). Racks drawn on the guides as in the patent figure.

claim: Instantaneous (grab-and-hold) car safety gear is allowed only up to 0.63 m/s rated speed; faster lifts need progressive gear
source_quote: Car safety gear: a) shall be of the progressive type, or b) may be of the instantaneous type if the rated speed of the lift does not exceed 0,63 m/s.
note: EN 81-20 5.6.2.1.2.1. Second: PFB: instantaneous 'brings the installation to an abrupt and immediate stop', 'rated speeds up to 0.63 m/s'.

claim: Progressive gear must slow a falling car on average between 0.2 g and 1 g; at the hardest (1 g average) a passenger feels about twice their weight
source_quote: For progressive safety gear the average retardation in the case of free fall of the car with rated load … shall lie between 0,2 gn and 1 gn.
note: EN 81-20 5.6.2.1.3. Felt load = 1 g + retardation (derived; research/model.py felt_max = 2).

claim: Disc springs behind the jaws set the clamping force, and the clamping force sets the deceleration
source_quote: the compression applied by the safety gear to the guide rail is set by means of a spring … the magnitude of the compressive force determines the deceleration of the elevator
note: KONE US 6,109,398. Second: Wittur ('braking force is adjustable by the disc spring assembly'); Otis US 10,407,278 (disc springs on the counter wedge).

claim: With a steady squeeze, the slowing is fairly steady (friction also varies with heat and speed)
source_quote: an acceleration value is substantially stabilized at approximately 0.9 g
note: Otis test of its design; friction = μN with N set by the springs (KONE). Shown as a flat retardation line, MODEL. VO v3 hedges 'fairly steady' (panel round 1, Katrin).

claim: From 2 m/s, the car stops in about 0.2 m (1 g) to 1 m (0.2 g), depending on the spring setting and the load in the car
source_quote: average retardation … shall lie between 0,2 gn and 1 gn
note: DERIVED: d = v²/2a = 0.20–1.02 m (research/model.py). HUD: MODEL. Load: net retardation = braking force / mass − g, so a fuller car slows less for the same springs (derived, model.py).

claim: The wedges scrape the rail: one maker's manual says the braking is friction plus metal cutting in the rail surface ('steel being shaved'); the marks are ground smooth afterward
source_quote: The braking effect is caused by metal cutting in the rail surface, friction and spring tensioning work. … the braking marks have to be grinded down.
note: SLC BF_D-1 manual. The manual's third item ('spring tensioning work') is left out: springs store energy rather than absorb it (panel round 1).

claim: The gear can only be released by raising the car, and a competent person must return the lift to service
source_quote: The release and automatic reset of a safety gear on the car … shall only be possible by raising the car … it shall require the intervention of a competent maintenance person to return the lift to service.

claim: A traction elevator's counterweight usually weighs the car plus about 40–50 % of the rated load
source_quote: equal to the weight of the car containing about 45% of its rated load
note: Barkand, MSHA. Second: TK Elevator Classroom on Demand (cab weight + 40–50 % of rated load); the balance minimises motor torque and energy (Inventio patent US 8,109,369: 'energetically advantageous').

claim: So an empty car is lighter than its counterweight; on a loss of control the counterweight can descend and pull the car up toward the overhead
source_quote: Where the combined mass of the elevator car and the passengers is less than the mass of the counter-balance, a loss in system control may cause the counter-balance to descend and the elevator car to ascend.
note: MSHA (as quoted in search; the fetched page confirms the 45 % balance and the overhead strikes). Causes: 'electrical, mechanical, and structural failures'.

claim: Classic car safeties do not protect in the upward direction
source_quote: do not provide protection in the upward direction
note: MSHA. VO: 'the classic safety gear' (modern gears exist that grip both ways: C29).

claim: A US study of mine elevators counted at least 18 ascending elevators striking the overhead in five years
source_quote: at least 18 documented cases of ascending elevators striking the overhead
note: MSHA, Barkand: 'Over a five-year period in the USA … counter-weighted elevators'. Told plainly, no names; no injuries claimed.

claim: Canada's elevator code made ascending car overspeed protection a rule in 1990
source_quote: went into effect April 1, 1990
note: CSA-B44 rule (three pages), per MSHA.

claim: Europe's code requires ascending car overspeed protection on traction lifts; a governor commonly detects it and triggers something that grips, for example a rope brake or safety gear that grips both ways
source_quote: Excessive speed in up direction (traction lifts only) — Ascending car overspeed protection means (5.6.6)
note: EN 81-20 Table 11. Rope brake: MSHA ('rope brake … overspeed in the upward and downward directions'). Two-way gear: SLC BF2D-1 'Braking up- and downwards'. Governor for upward overspeed: Tanno, 'Understanding the Requirements of the New EN-81 Standards' (Lift and Escalator Library): 'it is fairly standard practice to use an overspeed governor to detect excessive speed and then trigger a rope brake or safety gear upon detection' (https://liftescalatorlibrary.org/paper_indexing/papers/00000120.pdf).

claim: The counterweight hangs on the other end of the same ropes over the machine's sheave, so when the car goes up the counterweight comes down (said: 'every time you go up, it comes down')
source_quote: the counterweight can descend and pull the car up
note: Mechanism already drawn in s14 (ropes over the sheave); the MSHA paper's runaway description is the same coupling. Rope over a sheave: equal and opposite travel.

claim: The governor wheel turns whenever the car moves, because its rope is hooked to the car (said: 'it turns every time your car moves')
source_quote: is also connected to the elevator car 12, ensuring that the angular velocity of the tripping sheave 18 is related to the speed of the elevator car 12
note: Same mechanism as C06 and the line 'wherever your car goes, the rope goes too, and the wheel spins'.
